title: Test-first, A/B testing, validation and verification
blurb: Explain test or check first, A/B testing, TDD and BDD, and tell validation (right thing) from verification (thing right).
question: A team wants to know whether users prefer a one-page or a three-step booking form, and separately whether the form meets its specification. Which testing ideas apply to each?

teach.h: Decide early how you will test
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile asks the project to decide early how much testing and quality checking can be done the preferred agile way, 'test or check first', or at least 'test or check as you go'. This is one area where ideas from software need careful transfer: software can be built and tested with automation in days, hours or even minutes; other products, such as a marketing campaign, may not be built that quickly or automatically.

What it does

Right thing, and thing built right
teach.caption: From 9.4.3 and the Glossary; record the chosen methods in the quality management approach.

teach.body: Validation asks: are we building the right thing, the product users actually need? Verification asks: are we building the thing right, does it meet its specification and standards? Together they are sometimes called V&V. A product can pass verification perfectly and still fail validation if it solves the wrong problem.

A/B testing compares two versions of a product, design or feature to find out which is more effective. Different options are shown to users and their responses are analysed to guide the decision. It suits products such as web pages, emails or campaigns, where real user behaviour is the best evidence of what works.

Kestrel Valley Railway is rebuilding its online booking. Tester Ewan Gallagher writes automated checks from each story's acceptance criteria before developers build it: test first. To decide between a one-page and a three-step form, product owner Mei Lin shows each version to half of the visitors for a fortnight: an A/B test. Passing all checks verifies the form; the A/B result and demo feedback validate that it is the form passengers want.

teach.text: Validation = the RIGHT THING (user need). Verification = the THING RIGHT (specification). And test or check first is not limited to software: it can be applied to other products, but with care, because they may not be built quickly or with automation.

teach.body: The agile testing methods chosen, including those used by suppliers, are recorded in the quality management approach. Testers design, execute and possibly automate tests and quality reviews, building quality assurance into each iteration and checking products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team DoD.

summary: You can now explain test or check first and test or check as you go, TDD, BDD and A/B testing. You can also tell validation (building the right thing) from verification (building the thing right).

options: Testing each unit of code before it is written
Comparing two versions with users to see which works better
Checking a product against the team Definition of Done
Reviewing a product's design before any build starts
A.why: A/B testing compares two versions of a product, design or feature by presenting them to users and analysing their responses (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Writing unit tests before code is test-driven development.
whyNot.2: Checking against the team DoD is part of quality control by the tester.
whyNot.3: Reviewing a design before building is a quality review, not a comparison of two versions with users.

options: Are we building the thing right?
Are we building it within budget?
Are we building the right thing?
Are we building it on schedule?
A.why: Validation is about building the right thing; verification is about building the thing right (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Building the thing right is verification.
whyNot.1: Staying within budget is a cost question for progress control.
whyNot.3: Keeping to schedule is a time question for progress control.

A.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest deciding early about testing?
options: How much can be test or check first, or as you go
Which supplier will run the final acceptance test
How many testers each team needs for the project
Which iteration will hold the main test phase
A.why: A decision should be made early on how much testing and quality checking can be done test or check first, or at least test or check as you go (9.4.3).

whyNot.1: Agile does not rely on one final acceptance test; acceptance is frequent.
whyNot.2: Team size is an organization matter, not the testing decision described.
whyNot.3: Agile avoids a single late test phase; checking happens as work is built.

B.q: A charity plans to test its new donation email, not software. What does PRINCE2 Agile say about using test or check first here?
options: It cannot be used because it needs code
It replaces the need for user acceptance
It must be fully automated to count
It can be used, adapted with care
B.why: Test or check first can be used for other products, such as a campaign, but the transfer from software needs care because they may not be built as quickly or via automation (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: The book says the approach can be used for other products, not just code.
whyNot.1: Testing early does not replace user acceptance of the product.
whyNot.2: Non-software products may not be built via automation, yet checks can still come first.

B.q: Which technique is related to the test-first programming of eXtreme Programming and usually works at unit-testing level?
B.why: TDD relates to XP's test-first programming, requires automation and usually takes place at unit-testing level (Glossary).

whyNot.0: BDD builds on TDD in a wider, collaborative context using users' language.
whyNot.1: A/B testing compares two versions with users.
whyNot.3: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Verification checks that the product is built right.
2. Validation checks that the product meets its coding standard.
3. BDD uses language that users can understand easily.
4. A/B testing measures a team's velocity across iterations.
B.why: Verification is building the thing right (1), and BDD uses language users understand (3) (9.4.3, Glossary).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: meeting a standard is verification; validation is about the right thing.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: validation concerns user need, and A/B testing compares versions with users.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: A/B testing compares two versions, it does not measure velocity.

C.q: A team shows half of its website visitors one sign-up page and half another, then keeps the one that converts better. Which technique is this, and which question of V&V does it mainly help answer?
options: Test-driven development; building the thing right
Behaviour-driven development; building it on time
A/B testing; building the right thing
C.why: Comparing two versions with users is A/B testing, and evidence of what users respond to helps validate that the right thing is being built (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: TDD writes unit tests before code; it verifies, it does not compare versions with users.
whyNot.1: Refactoring changes structure without changing behaviour; it does not compare versions.
whyNot.2: BDD expresses tests in user language; V&V does not concern schedule.

C.q: A supplier will use automated test-first methods. Where are these recorded, and which role designs and runs the tests in the team?
C.why: Agile testing methods, including suppliers', are recorded in the quality management approach, and testers design, execute and possibly automate the tests (Table 9.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The commercial approach covers procurement and contracts; developers build rather than test.
whyNot.2: The quality register records results, not methods, and the team coach does not run tests.
whyNot.3: The product backlog holds stories, not testing methods, and the PO does not run the tests.

C.q: A form passes every check against its specification, but in the demo users say it does not let them do what they need. Which has passed and which has failed?
options: Test first passed; acceptance criteria failed
C.why: Meeting the specification shows it was built right (verification), but not meeting user need shows it is not the right thing (validation) (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: This reverses them: checks against specification are verification; user need is validation.
whyNot.2: No versions were compared and no restructuring took place.
whyNot.3: The checks against the specification passed, so its criteria were met; the gap is user need.

reteach.title: The wedding cake
reteach.question: How do you remember which of V&V is which?

blocks.body: A baker makes a flawless three-tier chocolate cake that matches the recipe exactly: built right, so verification passes. But the couple asked for lemon: wrong cake, so validation fails. Asking guests to taste two sample cakes and picking the favourite is A/B testing. Checking the sponge as each tier bakes is check as you go.

rows.label: Cake example
values: Is it the cake they wanted?

blocks.text: Validation: is it the right cake for the customer (the right thing)? Verification: was it made correctly to the recipe (the thing right)?

explain.body: Define the check before building, or at least check as you go. Decide early how much of each the project can do.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. The preferred agile way of quality checking is test or check [?], or at least test or check as you go.
test.why: The preferred agile manner is test or check first, or at least test or check as you go (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Checking at the end is the late-quality problem agile tries to avoid.
whyNot.2: The board does not carry out product checks.
whyNot.3: Checking after release is too late for the preferred approach.

explain.body: TDD is test-first at unit level from XP and needs automation. BDD builds on TDD, is more collaborative and is written in language users understand.

test.q: Which technique builds on TDD, is more collaborative and uses language users can easily understand?
test.why: Behaviour-driven development (BDD) is based on TDD, more collaborative, and uses language users understand (Glossary).

whyNot.0: TDD is the unit-level test-first technique that BDD builds on, not the extension itself.
whyNot.1: A/B testing compares two versions with users.
whyNot.3: XP (eXtreme Programming) is the agile approach whose test-first programming TDD relates to.

explain.body: Compare two versions of a product, design or feature with users and analyse their responses to decide which is more effective.

test.q: What guides the decision in an A/B test?
options: The users' responses to each version
The number of defects in each version
test.why: A/B testing presents different options to users and analyses their responses to guide decision-making (9.4.3).

whyNot.1: Effort estimates guide planning, not an A/B decision.
whyNot.2: The point is evidence from users, not the board's preference.
whyNot.3: Defect counts are verification evidence, not what an A/B test compares.

explain.body: Validation: building the right thing. Verification: building the thing right. Both are needed.

test.why: Verification is building the thing right; validation is building the right thing (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Building the right thing is validation.
whyNot.2: Speed is not what verification checks.
whyNot.3: Cost is not what verification checks.
